title: ‘Unlike Anything Else’: As ‘GTA 6’ Approaches, the Gaming Industry Braces the World for Its Pop Culture Takeover
description: There’s only so many times that gaming industry analysts can say “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be the biggest entertainment release of all time before
body:
There’s only so many times that gaming industry analysts can say “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be the biggest entertainment release of all time before the phrase seemingly loses all meaning to those who have never played a “GTA” game before.

	With just one week left until the Nov. 19 release of the most-anticipated video game release ever, everyone from the bystanders passing Vice City billboards and watching “SNL” sketches to Hollywood execs who’d seen Netflix’s “extended look” back in August knows the hottest topic right now is the Rockstar Games title. According to market research firm Newzoo, the game is currently estimated to bring in $3.25 billion to $5.2 billion in first week sales across PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S gaming consoles on a reported $1.5 billion budget.
	

	“Even if you don’t play games, chances are you’ve heard it,” Netflix’s vice president of nonfiction series Brandon Riegg tells Variety. “Just like maybe you’ve heard of a famous athlete or you’ve heard a famous song. So I think they had that in their favor.”



	

					Rockstar Games
	



	But not everyone knows what it is about “GTA 6” that will take up pop culture’s collective attention (and money), and those who do are very likely already off in the massive echo chamber that has been waiting for the game for 13 years. 

	The simplest possible answer is that the “Grand Theft Auto” franchise created a new type of video game, the open-world genre, and that new kind of video game has steadily grown to become the most immersive form of entertainment we have today. In these games, you have almost limitless possibilities for how you interact with the virtual world, making the normally collective experience of consuming the same piece of narrative media a personalized one as well.
	

	“Really, ‘GTA’ was the pioneer of the open-world game,” Game Awards creator, host and longtime gaming industry journalist Geoff Keighley tells Variety. “‘GTA 3,’ that’s really where Rockstar crossed over to do a 3D open-world game. So many games are so linear, where they are effectively scripts that you’re playing through and having a little bit of choice. But ‘GTA’ revolutionized the industry with a true open-world game that let you decide what journey you wanted to go on inside of this simulated environment. When ‘GTA 3’ came out, that was ahead of its time. And Rockstar has, with every game, the ambition has gotten bigger and bigger and bigger about what the density of the simulated world is. And that allows players to have a huge sense of agency to create the story that they want to create inside the world.”

	Riegg, who collaborated with Rockstar Games studio director Jennifer Kolbe to launch the “GTA 6” extended trailer in what he says “wasn’t a monetary sort of deal,” says “the game itself is probably the closest thing to this full immersion in this video game world.”

	“It’s ‘Ready Player One,’ maybe without the headset,” Riegg says. “There is a narrative to the game and objectives, but you can also just live in that world. You don’t have to do that stuff. I can have a relationship with somebody. I can text them. I can do crimes. It’s this immersive alternate universe that you can actually participate in in whatever way that you choose.”

	Strauss Zelnick, the head of Rockstar Games parent company Take-Two Interactive, says he has “so many thoughts” about the game, but he’s at a loss for new words until it’s unveiled.

	“It’s a nice question to ask,” Zelnick told Variety Monday when asked if there was anything specific that the Take-Two CEO feels he and the team at Rockstar haven’t said yet about “GTA 6” that they can say about the game before it’s out. “No, I mean I think our point of view has been well represented, and I think at this point, I put myself in the camp of cautiously optimistic.”



	

					Rockstar Games
	



	Zelnick, formerly the president of 20th Century Fox and head of BMG Entertainment, has done so many “GTA 6” preview interviews at this point that apart from recently defending Take-Two’s track record with hit franchises (“GTA,” “Red Dead Redemption,” “NBA 2K,” “Borderlands” and “Sid Meier’s Civilization”) in a conversation with the Wall Street Journal, not much has changed between Q&As.
	

	“Everyone here is incredibly excited about the upcoming launch,” Zelnick says. “Pre-orders are running far in excess of our expectations, so that’s a good thing. That said, we never claim success before it occurs, so we’re just days away from beginning to see the fruits of our labor.”

	“GTA 6” is a guaranteed hit (“Lord knows I need it,” Zelnick joked) so measuring the $80 game’s success is going to go well beyond analyzing financials and into hours played, time spent away from other forms of entertainment and the percentage of the workforce that takes the day off. And that last one is no joke.

	“I honestly think hardly anyone in the gaming industry is going to be working that day,” says Christoph Hartmann, the former head of Take-Two Interactive’s 2K Games and currently the chief at Ubisoft’s Massive Entertainment.

	“I actually downloaded it today, and I’m upset because the Wi-Fi went really slow in our house,” Hartmann told Variety Wednesday. “I think it was 212 GBs. And yes, I’m gonna take a day off, and then I have the challenge about my 14-year-old son insisting he can play as well, and I told him it’s mature, and I he said, ‘Yeah, but Dad, you worked on that game. Shouldn’t I know what it is?'”



	

					Rockstar Games
									Rockstar Games
	



	“Grand Theft Auto 6” is the story of Jason and Lucia, a pair that “have always known the deck is stacked against them,” per Rockstar Games. “But when an easy score goes wrong, they find themselves on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America, in the middle of a criminal conspiracy stretching across the state of Leonida – forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.”

	Rockstar Games co-studio head Rob Nelson has said the game’s main narrative should take approximately 80 hours to play through. The title will have the largest open-world map in the franchise’s history and offer new ways for players to shape their gameplay, from deciding the level of romance between Jason and Lucia to what their physiques look like based on what they eat and how often they work out.

	“‘GTA’ games have been unique in their ambition, and certainly this one. The scale of what they built over a decade is incredible,” Keighley says. “So I think that’s why players respond to these games, because there’s just so much possibility inside the world of how you play it. This is not a game that you play in 20 hours and finish. You continue to exist in this world and explore it. And obviously, ‘GTA Online,’ that’s been a big thing that continued to go on for a decade. So the ‘GTA’ experience is unlike anything else in gaming, much less entertainment. That’s what is so unique about the ‘GTA’ games, is that they really are peerless across all of entertainment because of the scale.”
	

	Since its founding by brothers Dan Houser and Sam Houser in 1998, Rockstar Games has become the “largest American games publisher” and owns “the largest entertainment franchise” with “Grand Theft Auto 6,” according to SuperData CEO and NYU “Business of Video Games” professor Joost Van Dreunen.



	

					Rockstar Games
									Rockstar Games
	



	On the massive success of “Red Dead Redemption 2” and “Grand Theft Auto 5,” “they’re not the underdog” anymore, Van Dreunen notes, meaning a big part of Rockstar’s counter-culture appeal has gone mainstream since its last hit released. “So can it maintain that character, and can it commercialize that?” Van Dreunen asks.

	“GTA 6” will launch amid Rockstar Games workers’ continued efforts to unionize, now with public support from SAG-AFTRA. The timing isn’t a coincidence, with Rockstar employees aiming to call attention to their detailed work over the past 13 years while Take-Two Interactive is poised to make billions off their labor. The success of the game is likely to impact the gaming industry at large, as well as how the general public views the medium, which has long struggled to be taken as seriously as movies and TV despite the more than $200 billion in revenue games bring in each year.

	“My hope is that they’ve taken the success of ‘GTA 5’ to manifest the creative vision that they had in their head this whole time, have really delivered on that,” Van Dreunen says. “And I think that will be its unique selling point, not the fact that it’s this sort of fringe form of entertainment and my mom tells me I’m not allowed to play this game. That was a big part of its selling point, its marketing. They used to guerrilla marketing. They would have stickers in Lower Manhattan and the East Village, these Rockstar stickers everywhere on lamp posts and on street furniture and all that stuff. They would take a very rebellious approach to marketing because it’s in line and on brand with the game.”

schema.headline: ‘Unlike Anything Else’: As ‘GTA 6’ Approaches, the Gaming Industry Braces the World for Its Pop Culture Takeover

title: Chris Colfer Says ‘Glee’ Reboot ‘Conversations’ About Kurt’s Return Are Ongoing: ‘From What I Heard, It Sounded Very Funny and Like a Good Idea’
description: Chris Colfer confirmed on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed: The Podcast” that he is having conversations about returning as Kurt Hummel in the “Glee” re
body:
Chris Colfer confirmed on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed: The Podcast” that he is having conversations about returning as Kurt Hummel in the “Glee” reboot that is now in development at Disney+ and Hulu. News of the revival broke in late October, with Variety reporting soon after that original cast member Lea Michele is set to return as Rachel Berry. Considering the close bond between Kurt and Rachel, “Glee” fans have been wondering if the reboot would also bring Kurt back.
	

	While stopping short of confirming his return, Colfer cryptically said he’s had a “nice conversation with someone” about the “Glee” reboot and “I’m gonna have more conversations soon,” adding: “From what I heard, it sounded very funny and it sounded like a good idea. So we’ll see.”

	“At this point I’m just curious,” Colfer said about the reboot. “We did so much stuff that was that was revolutionary and groundbreaking at the time. I’d be very curious to see how they keep that up.”

	Colfer starred as Kurt on all six seasons of “Glee,” which ran on Fox from 2009 to 2015. His performance won him the Golden Globe for best supporting actor in a television series and earned him two supporting actor nominations at the Emmys. The character wrapped the series married to his longtime boyfriend Blaine Anderson (Darren Criss), with Rachel as the surrogate for their child. If Kurt does return to the reboot, Colfer said he wants to see the character “in a place of power.”

	“I would love to see him like a Miranda Priestly-type, running his own fashion blog or a magazine,” the actor said. “I could also see him on tour with Chappell Roan, styling her. There’s a lot of fun avenues they could explore.”
	

	The reboot might also plan to explore Kurt and Blaine’s lives as parents, to which Colfer said: “I’m sure he and Blaine would have very different parenting techniques. I think Blaine would be a gentle parent, and Kurt would not. I think Kurt would punish his children with scathing looks.”

	Colfer was also asked about the prospect of making a “Glee” reboot in the wake of so much tragedy that has befallen the cast. Cory Monteith, who played Finn Hudson, died after Season 4 from an accidental overdose of heroin and alcohol, while Santana Lopez actor Naya Rivera died in 2020 at 33 years old after she drowned while saving her four-year-old son.

	“It was really hard going back to the show after Cory passed, and I’m sure it’d be really difficult, especially now that Naya’s gone too,” Colfer said. “But I guess you have to think, are you going to let the loss of two people you love very much prevent you from being around a dozen other people you love as well? There’s a lot to think about with it.”

	Head over to The Daily Beast’s website to listen to the full podcast interview with Colfer.

schema.headline: Chris Colfer Says ‘Glee’ Reboot ‘Conversations’ About Kurt’s Return Are Ongoing: ‘From What I Heard, It Sounded Very Funny and Like a Good Idea’

title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Lists Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman Among 10 Writers
description:
The chances that Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman could be back as Deadpool and Wolverine in “Avengers: Doomsday” may be getting higher.

	Eagle-eyed
body:
The chances that Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman could be back as Deadpool and Wolverine in “Avengers: Doomsday” may be getting higher.

	Eagle-eyed Marvel fans combed through the Writer’s Guild of America’s directory and spotted the screenwriting credits for “Doomsday,” which lists Reynolds and Jackman among the 10 writers who contributed to the movie. Notably, Reynolds was one of the writers on “Deadpool 2” and “Deadpool & Wolverine,” while this marks Jackman’s first writing credit.
	

	The main feature writing credits on “Doomsday” go to Marvel veteran Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron, creator of “Loki” and writer of “Doctor Strange Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.” The credits for additional literary materials (not on screen) go to McFeely, Waldron, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Reynolds and Jackman.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” director Cretton had originally been tapped to helm the film when it was known as “The Kang Dynasty” with Loveness to write — but it was later reworked after Kang the Conqueror actor Jonathan Majors was fired by Disney. After Cretton had stepped down from the film, the Russo Bros. came on board with McFeely, McKenna, Sommers and Waldron to shift the focus to Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom as the main villain.

	Variety has reached out to reps for Marvel, Reynolds and Jackman for comment. Reynolds also appeared to weigh in on the writing credits with a cryptic X post of a video from “Deadpool & Wolverine.”


	The writing credits for Reynolds and Jackman certainly seem like they would be for writing dialogue for their “X-Men” characters, but it’s unclear if or how much they would appear in “Doomsday.” The website defines the additional literary material as “an official film credit introduced by the Writers Guild of America to recognize Guild-contracted writers who contributed writing services to a theatrical feature but did not qualify for a traditional primary writing credit.”
	

	The WGA directory also has this caveat: “The information contained in the ‘Find a Writer’ database is the most current and accurate available to Writers Guild of America West (WGAW) and Writers Guild of America, East (WGAE). Some of the data is self-reported by writers and not independently verified by WGAW and WGAE. Users of the database accept the data as is, with no warranty of its accuracy stated or implied.”

schema.headline: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Lists Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman Among 10 Writers

title: Drama Writers Talk Casting the Perfect Actor and the Pressures of Showrunning: ‘People Are Looking at You to Steer the Story’
description: Whether it’s waiting on a renewal for another season or tackling how to extend a character’s storyline, TV drama creators are almost always dealing
body:
Whether it’s waiting on a renewal for another season or tackling how to extend a character’s storyline, TV drama creators are almost always dealing with perpetual stress. Katori Hall, the creator, executive producer and showrunner of “P-Valley,” decided to unwind between seasons this year by getting her pilot’s license.

	“Only a showrunner would relax by getting their pilot’s license,” Elizabeth Meriwether, the executive producer and creator of “Furious,” quipped at Variety’s annual Night in the Writers’ Room: Awards Season Edition.
	

	While this achievement was unique to Hall, the other six panelists all rejoiced over the feeling of having that one actor that they wrote a role for and took forever to sign on. For Meriwether and Hall, this is a result of their backgrounds in theater, where they instantly “fall in love with actors.”

	“Am I an actor whore?” Hall joked. “I guess I am. Just beautiful performers that you want to be a part of your tribe, and you want to grow with them and give them an opportunity to grow and give them really amazing work.”

	The actress in question, for both Hall and “The Drop: A Snowfall Saga” creator, executive producer and writer Malcolm Spellman, was Gail Bean.

	“She is so good at embodying that same spirit that she sort of just saved the country,” Spellman said. “She really brings that indomitableness to it.”

	For Meriwether, it was Steve Way. “Steve was on a panel [about caretaking in television] and his whole bit was that he didn’t have work and he couldn’t pay for his wheelchair, and I was in the writers’ room for ‘Furious,’ like, ‘I can give him work,’” Meriwether said. Once she gave him the job, he slowly unveiled hidden details about his life in his wheelchair, and she was able to incorporate his experiences into the role of Alden.
	

	Brad Caleb Kane, the creator, writer, showrunner and executive producer of “Crystal Lake,” knew he needed Linda Cardellini among his cast. “They sent me lists of people, and I said, ‘The only one I want for this is Linda Cardellini because as we write these scripts, I see her. I want her and I want to write to her strengths going forward,’” Kane said. Luckily for him, Cardellini agreed after a lengthy five-and a-half hour discussion about the character.

	With “Lanterns,” creator, writer and executive producer Chris Mundy bends both his characters and his writers’ room according to those around him to maximize the number of perspectives told in his story. “We’d be doing a really bad job if we weren’t taking the things they’re bringing and incorporating them and growing,” Mundy said.

	These creators wouldn’t have the authority to command talent without having worked their way up to the showrunner position. While they are willing to compromise and hear the ideas of their fellow staffers, they have final say.

	“It’s a very sobering experience when you realize you’re number one,” said Ben Watkins, creator, writer, director and executive producer of “The Greatest.” “The amount of pressure that you feel from deadlines or budgets or just being in that seat and having everybody saying, ‘Where are we going?’ There is some pressure, and it will change you and I think it’s really important to acknowledge that.”

	Kane echoed Watkins’ sentiment but acknowledged the importance of collaboration.

	“Good leadership is obviously you’re the captain of the ship, and people are looking at you to steer the story to its ultimate destination, but if you’re smart enough to hire people who have really good ideas and they almost inevitably are going to have some ideas that are better than yours, that’s what makes it a collective and a room. Part of the skill set is learning to put your ego aside and and and be able to hear better ideas that serve the story,” Kane said.

	This collaborative spirit was not the circumstance for Hall when she was finding her footing as a staff writer. Similar to Kane, she knew when she became the leader, her writers’ room would be different.

	“As I moved up and grew into my showrunnern-ess, I always felt that everyone’s voice was equal. I wanted the staff writer on my show to feel as if they could speak, not as much as me, but maybe as much as the co-EP,” Hall said.
	

	Meriwether uniquely did not start as a staff writer but jumped right into the seat of showrunner at 29-years-old. She found her voice — figuratively — working long hours through the grind that is network television.

	“I lost my voice, and they and I went to the doctor and the doctor was like, ‘Have you been drinking a lot of coffee and or trying to sound authoritative?’ I was like, ‘Yes, both of those’ and then I twinkled that experience into ‘The Dropout,’” Meriwether said.

	Coincidentally, Watkins and Spellman got their early starts in Hollywood alongside each other and found themselves reunited at the panel, celebrating their growth in the industry 40 years later.

	“Our journey is so intertwined,” Spellman said. “We’ve handed our pilots back and forth to each other, our wives are tight, the struggle was so real for us for so fucking long, so it means a lot.”

schema.headline: Drama Writers Talk Casting the Perfect Actor and the Pressures of Showrunning: ‘People Are Looking at You to Steer the Story’

title: David Walliams Adaptation ‘Fing!’ Pulled by Doha Film Festival Following Sexual Harassment Allegations
description: The upcoming Doha Film Festival has removed fantasy feature “Fing!” from its program following sexual misconduct allegations against David Walliams
body:
The upcoming Doha Film Festival has removed fantasy feature “Fing!” from its program following sexual misconduct allegations against David Walliams, the British actor and writer who is the author of the book on which the film is based.

	Walliams, who rose to prominence for his comedy show “Little Britain” before becoming a judge on “Britain’s Got Talent,” has recently been accused of grooming fans as young as 15 in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, who allege the comedian invited teenage girls over to his house, where they stayed over, and to his dressing rooms. They also allege he would “pester” and “pressure” young women, including models and an employee at his publisher HarperCollins, to go out with him and in some cases even take part in sexual activity.
	

	Walliams denies the allegations.

	The Doha Film Festival’s removal of “Fing!” is the latest in a series of removals of Walliams-related content from various outlets, starting with the BBC which has announced it is pulling shows, including “Little Britain,” that star or were written by the British comedian, from its streaming platform. Meanwhile Comcast-owned Sky has pulled out as the U.K. and Ireland broadcaster for “Fing!,” which is directed by Jeffrey Walker. The film world premiered positively at Sundance and was set to have its international launch in Doha.

	The revamped Doha Film Festival has transformed the DFI’s existing Ajyal Film Festival, dedicated to youth and family-friendly cinema, into a more ambitious international event for a broader audience.
	

	Walliams wrote the children’s book on which “Fing!” is based, co-wrote the screenplay and cameos in the fantasy feature alongside main stars Taika Waititi, Mia Wasikowska and Iona Bell.

	“Fing!” is produced by AGC Studios, Bondit Media Capital in L.A., Elevate Media Production in Australia and Walliams’ production company King Bert.

	Ticketholders for the “Fing!” gala event in Doha have been informed that the screening has been cancelled and that they will receive full refunds, a festival rep. confirmed to Variety.

	The Doha Film Festival will run in the Qatari capital Nov. 19-27.

schema.headline: David Walliams Adaptation ‘Fing!’ Pulled by Doha Film Festival Following Sexual Harassment Allegations

title: Alanis Morissette Slams Ben Affleck for ‘Asking Why I Didn’t Lead With My Sexuality,’ Then Plays Video at Concert of His Head Exploding
description:
Alanis Morissette did not hold back when recalling the words of her “Dogma” co-star, Ben Affleck. 

	During the Nov. 11 date of her “Butterfly With
body:
Alanis Morissette did not hold back when recalling the words of her “Dogma” co-star, Ben Affleck. 

	During the Nov. 11 date of her “Butterfly With a Machete” residency at the YouTube Theater in Inglewood, Calif., the singer spoke pointedly about Affleck during a monologue about “harsh judgments” she felt being in the public eye (via Entertainment Weekly).

	“I’ve even had a guy ask me why I didn’t lead with my sexuality,” she said. “Thank you, Ben Affleck.”
	

	A video then showed a scene from “Dogma,” which Morissette and Affleck both starred in, where the latter’s head explodes. In the film, Morissette plays God, whose voice is so powerful that it instantly kills the fallen angel Bartleby, played by Affleck.

	Elsewhere in the concert, Morissette spoke more about being in the public eye, where she felt “harsh judgments about my songs, about my body, about how I look, about how I think, about how I feel, about my value system, about my weight, about how feral I am, about how feral I live, about my approach to parenting, about my approach to education, my approach to freaking anything.”

	She later spoke about an unsuccessful attempt at “looking for a friend” by trying to connect with a fellow star, saying, “I did call Johnny Depp at one point, and his response was, ‘Why are you calling me?’”

	Morissette’s “Butterfly With a Machete” residency just wrapped after its fourth and final show, following an initial run in Las Vegas last year.

	Variety reached out to Affleck’s representitive for comment, but no response was received by publish time.
	

	You can see the moment below, as captured on Entertainment Weekly’s Instagram.

schema.headline: Alanis Morissette Slams Ben Affleck for ‘Asking Why I Didn’t Lead With My Sexuality,’ Then Plays Video at Concert of His Head Exploding

title: Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s
description:
Jo Koy had a speech ready when he walked onstage in Stockton, Calif.

	It was his first time in the Central Valley city, and before taping the two
body:
Jo Koy had a speech ready when he walked onstage in Stockton, Calif.

	It was his first time in the Central Valley city, and before taping the two sold-out arena shows that became his new Netflix special, he went looking for its Filipino history. He found plenty: “No Filipinos allowed” signs on restaurants, water fountains Filipinos weren’t allowed to drink from and the Little Manila neighborhood later split by a freeway. “There were a lot of fucked-up things that happened,” he tells me, before apologizing for the language. “It just really sucked.”
	

	The plan was to open by hitting all of it hard. Then, the minute he walked out, the crowd gave him a standing ovation.

	“I saw this white guy high-five this Asian guy, and a Black guy was standing and this Black lady over here, Latinos over here and a Filipino right here,” he says. “And I was just like, no, man, I’m not gonna do this.” He made the call on the spot. “What happened in the past is the past, but look where we are now.”

	That’s what he brought to his comedy special “Jo Koy: Blue in the Face,” which premiered Sept. 15 on Netflix and completes the two-special deal he signed with the streamer in 2023. Koy edits his own specials, cutting two shows that each ran more than two hours down to 55 minutes and shaping the hour like a bookend around one idea: Keep your circle tight and celebrate the people who celebrated you.

	The special is a contender in the Golden Globes’ best performance in stand-up comedy on television category, and it will enter the Emmy race for outstanding variety special (pre-recorded) next year. Koy joined me for a conversation after a Variety Screening Series presentation of the special, and he came with plenty of stories.
	

	He talked about the phone call he got from Voletta Wallace, the Notorious B.I.G.’s mother, who died in February 2025, after he performed an uncleared Biggie bit in “Live From Brooklyn” and had to pay for the songs. He described a day at Amblin when everyone from the lobby to a hallway lined with Indiana Jones memorabilia told him “Steven” loved “Comin’ in Hot,” leaving him to wonder whether they meant someone in accounting. They meant Oscar-winning Steven Spielberg, and the meeting landed Koy the DreamWorks deal that became “Easter Sunday.”

	And of course, there’s his mother, the single mom who cursed out a man at a shoe store in 1984 for mocking her accent and who built her Filipino community by walking up to strangers at church.He also shared the origin of his stage name, which he didn’t understand until years later, over a meal at Long John Silver’s: His Auntie Evelyn had never called him “Jo Koy.” She was saying “Jo ko,” which means “my Jo” in Tagalog.

	Even the special’s title came by accident. His director, Shannon Hartman, suggested “Blue in the Face,” and the teal stage he nearly rejected happened to match it. Then fans started sending him photos of their dogs glued to the special, and his manager offered a theory about the color.

	“It’s all coming together,” Koy says.

	He also owes Variety some lumpia, preferably his mother’s.



	

	



	Why did you want to film the special in Stockton?

	On tour, you have your prime markets — the Bay Area, New York, L.A. — and people think a special has to be shot in a big market. But in these secondary markets, people come out, man. They want to go to a show and be a part of it. When I finally got to Stockton, people were like, “Oh, you’re going to Stockton? Be careful.” Then we sold out two arenas, and the crowd was amazing.

	It was my first time there, and I found so much Filipino history: the first immigrants who set foot there and the racism they had to put up with. Restaurants had “No Filipinos allowed” signs. They weren’t allowed to drink out of certain water fountains. They built Little Manila, and then that got displaced and a freeway went down the middle of it. A lot of fucked-up things happened. I’m sorry to curse. It just really sucked.So I wanted to shine a light on it. I wanted to come to this town and say, “I know what happened in the past was really bad, but look how far we’ve come as a people. Through all that adversity, now there’s a Filipino son up there and it’s like, hey, we did it.”
	

	Backstage, my plan was to come out and hit that hard, then ease into the special. And I swear to God, Clayton, the minute I walked out, they gave me a standing ovation. We didn’t ask for that. I saw this white guy high-five this Asian guy, and a Black guy was standing and this Black lady over here, Latinos over here and a Filipino right here. And I was just like, no, man, I’m not gonna do this. That’s not what this is. What happened in the past is the past, but look where we are now. Let’s take it from here. I made that decision onstage.

	You filmed over two nights. When you watch it back, can you tell which night is which?

	On all my specials, the second night is always the best because I got it out of the way. Whatever idea I had for the special, I get it out on the first night. The second night is where I have fun and freestyle. There were jokes that night I literally just came up with.

	Walk me through the life of a joke. Is there a four-hour Jo Koy cut out there somewhere?

	There’s a lot. Both shows were over two hours, and I cut it down to 55 minutes. I always want my specials to have a story — I know it sounds cheesy — like a bookend. I want to start here, have everything connect and end here. And this one, I really wanted Fred … [He pauses, tearing up.] God, I hate this.

	The whole story was keeping your circle tight. Get the crabs out of your life. Celebrate your wins and the people who celebrated you. That’s how I wanted to start and how I wanted to end. That was the whole idea behind “Blue in the Face.” All right, I’m done. Sorry about that.

	“Blue in the Face” completes the two-special deal you signed with Netflix in 2023. The first was “Live From Brooklyn.”

	I crushed Brooklyn, man. I did a Biggie bit there, and we weren’t supposed to because I’d never cleared the songs. I promised everyone I wouldn’t. Then I was in this Brooklyn moment, and as I’m doing it, I’m like, “Oh, fuck. I have to pay for these songs.” And we had to.

	But that bit went so huge that I ended up on the phone with Mrs. Wallace. She said, “Thank you for keeping my son’s legacy alive. It’ll always be on Netflix, and generations after this will always see his body of work. I love you for that.” And I go, “You’re welcome, Mrs. Wallace. He was a king, and he was my hero. And of course it’s going to be on Netflix, because you charged me so much money for this song.”
	

	She gave me the rights to his face, the one where he’s wearing a crown. I can use it forever. I never have to ask. And for every shirt, we donate to the Wallace Foundation.

	So what comes after this? A new deal, a new home, a break from the one-hour format?

	I haven’t signed another deal yet. This one just ended. But I love Netflix. I’ve known everybody over there for a long time, and creatively, they respect my decisions. It’s fun to submit something, and they press play.

	You also voice a character in “Forgotten Island.” After “Easter Sunday,” what did you learn about how Hollywood tells Filipino stories?

	Do you know how I got “Easter Sunday?” Steven Spielberg watched “Comin’ in Hot,” my special in Hawaii. We literally got a call, and that’s how I got my deal with DreamWorks. I pitched the idea that my mom and my aunt haven’t spoken in something like 25 years. I talk about it onstage, how every holiday I have to pick: “OK, I can go see Auntie Evelyn at 3, then come here for dinner at 6.” There’s constant drama in our family, but Easter Sunday is the one thing that finally brings us together.

	Then the pandemic hit the minute I got the deal. We shot in Vancouver when it opened up, with everyone six feet apart and auditions on Zoom. Then we waited for theaters to reopen, like everyone else, so we were up against all the movies that were supposed to come out before the pandemic. My release was with “Maverick,” “Jurassic World,” “Minions,” “Thor” and “Easter Sunday.” It was the craziest week. But I held on for three weeks, so that was dope.

	With “Forgotten Island,” I loved everything about it. We got to do an animated movie at a major studio with all these great people backing it. Plus, it’s the folklore. When I was a kid, that’s all I heard — don’t step on the duwende. And now here I am taking my kid to watch something my grandma used to talk about.

	Your mom has been your best character for 20 years. What was her review of this latest special?

	She always has one. And she’s big because of it. By the way, my impersonation of her is no caricature. It’s not exaggerated at all. If I’m next to her and you turn the lights off, you wouldn’t know who’s my mom. I’m not embellishing any stories. These are things my mom did, and I’m just reliving them.
	

	What’s your favorite mom story you’ve told?

	The shoe store. I was messing up the shoes, and the guy cursed at me and that pissed my mom off. She said, “Don’t talk to my son like that.” Then he made fun of her accent. It’s 1984, and he’s making fun of her to her face and she goes, “Oh, you’re making fun of my accent, huh? I speak two languages in your country, Tagalog and English. How many do you speak? One. You’re stupid.” To see my mom, a single mom, do that in the ’80s, you’re like, oh, fuck. That’s when I got scared of my mom. She never backed away from a fight.

	She was very prideful too. There was no Facebook, no Instagram. She had to find her community. We’d go to church, and she would literally walk up to brown people: “Pilipino ka? Pilipino rin ako.” And boom, now she’s got a friend. Those people are her best friends to this day. Then they started renting out the Knights of Columbus hall for potlucks, and all the kids would perform. I saw my mom’s hustle every Sunday, and I got excited because I got to hang out with other Filipino kids and eat food nobody knew about yet. Now everyone knows about Filipino food. Not back then.

	Deserted island. You can take three stand-up specials from all of history. What are they?

	Richard Pryor’s “Live in Concert,” the Long Beach one. I didn’t know what a comedian was until my neighbor gave me that tape and said, “No, you’re a comedian.” Then I was addicted to Richard.Then Eddie Murphy’s “Delirious.” People think he was a full-grown 40-year-old man. He was a kid right out of high school. Some of it’s a little immature — well, no shit, he’s a kid! But the way he owned that stage, and the confidence when he delivered his lines, was amazing. And he was so handsome. I wanted a red leather suit like this cat.

	Then Chris Rock’s “Bring the Pain.” It wasn’t only super funny; it was a cultural moment. He made everyone rethink and see things differently. And there are countless others. 

	10 QUESTIONS WITH JOY KOY

	Childhood nickname? 

	At school they called me Herbert. But my Auntie Evelyn calls me “Jo ko.” Her daughter Mona is my best friend, and when I was doing open mics as Joseph Herbert, they’d always make a joke or say it wrong. I told Mona, “I gotta change my name, dude.” And right then, Auntie Evelyn goes, “Jo ko, eat!” It sounded like “Jo Koy.” We both looked at each other: “Oh yeah. Jo Koy.”
	

	Years later, everyone kept asking me what “Jo Koy” meant and I’d say, “I don’t know. My aunt just calls me that.” So I took her out to eat and asked her why. She’s like, “I don’t call you Jo Koy. You keep fucking saying that. It’s ‘Jo ko.’” “Ko” means “my.” My Jo. We were at Long John Silver’s on Maryland Parkway, and I started crying.

	Karaoke or shower song?

	Karaoke would always be Harry Connick Jr.’s “We Are in Love.”

	Give me an alternate title for “Blue in the Face.”

	I wanted to call it “Live From Stockton.” 

	Secret talent?

	Editing. I crush it in the bay. I edit all my specials, and this one was like a puzzle because there were big bits. I don’t like obvious audience cuts, where you cut to the fans and, boom, now I’ve moved over to the left. I’ll find a way to merge two bits together through a camera. It takes a long, long time. I’ll be in that bay for days. No sleep. Just fart and spit.

	Favorite ice cream flavor?

	Peanut butter from McConnell’s, with dark chocolate. It’s like a frozen Reese’s. And I’m lactose intolerant, so I’m willing to sacrifice my stomach. I don’t care.

	One item you couldn’t live without?

	Oh, man. I guess tequila.

	What TV show or film in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of?

	“Beat Street.” Rocking a Kangol and some fat laces. That’d be sick.

	Which fictional character you most relate to or admire?

	That’s a tough one. I guess Bugs Bunny. That writing doesn’t exist anymore. Those guys were good. Sometimes racist, but if they could edit that part out.

	Favorite piece of advice you’ve given or received?

	Try everything. Whatever’s in your gut, do it. You only live once, so why listen to anything outside your gut? Whatever dream you have, pursue it and don’t listen to anybody else. And when you fall down and fail, get back up and do it again, because you’re doing something no one else did. You tried. Believe me, a lot of people are jealous when you try. They thrive on you failing, and they’re the first ones to speak up, because they’ll never try. I don’t want to live life going, “Oh, I wish I had done that.” I want to be like, “I did that.”

	Ooh, that was a bar. 
	

	The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

schema.headline: Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s

title: NBC News Will Cancel Streaming Show ‘Stay Tuned,’ Trim Some Positions in Staff Realignment
description: NBC News will cease airing its one hour of primetime programming on the “NBC News Now” streaming service as part of a review of its resources, acco
body:
NBC News will cease airing its one hour of primetime programming on the “NBC News Now” streaming service as part of a review of its resources, according to a person familiar with the matter — resulting in the end of “Stay Tuned,” a show that streamed from the West Coast at 8 p.m. ET, and the elimination of a handful of positions across the NBCUniversal news unit.

	Gadi Schwartz, the NBC News correspondent who anchored “Stay Tuned,” will continue to work for the news division, this person said. Producers who worked on the program will have the opportunity to apply for nearly 50 open positions that will be available at NBC News, this person says. Many of the roles involve working on “Dateline” or the news specials department and there is hope, this person says, that many of those affected will take up those positions.
	

	 A handful of NBC News employees, said to represent less than 1% of the overall staff, will have to deal with eliminated positions across the news unit, this person says.

	NBC News confirmed that Wednesday’s streaming of “Stay Tuned” was its last, but declined to make executives available for comment. NBC News Now is expected to fill its primetime schedule with re-airs of previous streaming programming. The service already repeats Tom Llamas’ streaming show, “Top Story,” in evening hours.

	NBC News isn’t the only TV-news division looking at staffing during a tricky era for media companies. Skydance, the owner of CNN and CBS News, has offered buyouts to staff across the company as part of a bid to seek $6 billion in cost cuts after amassing a mammoth amount of debt to combine Warner Bros. Discovery with Paramount. CBS News and CNN have had other rounds of layoffs in past months.
	

	The end of “Stay Tuned” isn’t seen as a reduction in commitment to free, ad-supported streaming. The streaming outlet, which counts Savannah Sellers, Joe Fryer, Christine Romans and Hallie Jackson among its anchors, saw viewing triple between 2020 and 2025.

schema.headline: NBC News Will Cancel Streaming Show ‘Stay Tuned,’ Trim Some Positions in Staff Realignment

title: ‘White Tiger Column’ Directors on How Myanmar’s Resistance Speaks to Political Youth Movements in Brazil, Serbia and the U.S.: ‘Revolution Is on the Lips of a Lot of People’
description: In 2021, 10 months after Myanmar’s military overthrew the democratically elected government in a coup, Canadian photojournalist Bryan Dickie heard
body:
In 2021, 10 months after Myanmar’s military overthrew the democratically elected government in a coup, Canadian photojournalist Bryan Dickie heard of a rare opening to access the country. He acted swiftly. The experience of that trip inspired him to enlist long-time collaborators Robert Mentov and Dwight Jantzi, with the trio returning to Myanmar two years later and capturing the training regime of young recruits of the People’s Defense Force. The result of the six weeks on the ground is “White Tiger Column,” opening this year’s International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam.
	

	For 45 days, the trio of filmmakers captured the lives of trainees and commanders as they readied to leave for the front and join the war. Through an observational lens, the directors reflect on the dichotomy of the situation: the mundanity of the lives of young kids who scroll on TikTok and sing mindlessly to Taylor Swift and Justin Bieber and the harsh reality of armed combat.

	Speaking with Variety ahead of heading to Amsterdam, Dickie mentions how he built “deep ties” with locals in Myanmar over 15 years of covering the area as a photojournalist. That, coupled with his close relationship with the Burmese diaspora in Canada, gave the filmmaker great knowledge of the country’s geopolitical situation. “I’ve also embedded with multiple different ethnic armed organizations over the years, so through all of that I built up a bit of a track record going into these areas.”

	“We just felt a clear creative collaboration,” adds Jantzi of the early days of working on the project. “Upon landing on the ground and shooting alongside each other, we were just working very closely, day by day, developing our shot list and working through our potential narrative arcs. Through Rob and my ongoing work as filmmakers and then Bryan and his deep knowledge of the context and the region, it just felt like a very cohesive, natural fit to work together.”
	

	Jantzi emphasizes the trio would have loved to have taken a few more trips to the country during development and shooting, but the situation was too precarious to allow the extra time. “The reality is that the situation changes so much week by week that you can’t even really plan your characters six months ahead,” he notes. “We got extremely lucky with timing and kept trying to extend our trip, and things kept changing and becoming a bit more contentious in the region.”

	That sensitivity extends to the subject of the documentary itself, with the directors keenly aware of the cultural and political nuances the project involved. Mentov mentions how the trio worked closely with the diaspora, as well as fellow Burmese filmmakers on the ground. “One thing we wanted to do was to maintain this observational approach.”

	“Essentially, we were just dropped into this jungle,” he goes on. “We were trying to understand it, but it was very similar to how the recruits were: dropped into the jungle and trying to understand it all. Cinematically, we really just wanted to film these conversations at a distance and give space for them as opposed to trying to drive a narrative in more of a traditional documentary style.”

	That desire is clearly reflected in the film’s visual and narrative language, with “White Tiger Column” foregoing traditional talking heads or extensive voice-overs cueing the viewer into minute details of the conflict in favor of letting the camera linger on seemingly mundane activities made poignant in this very specific context. The filmmakers also shot on longer lenses and employed a locked-off tripod technique to keep the camera static for stretched periods.



	

					Courtesy of IDFA
	



	Another “conscious” decision was to avoid showcasing explicit violence, with the film focusing instead on the training and conversations revolving around conflict. “We talked a lot about wanting to make a war film that didn’t show war,” notes Dickie.

	“I found it very hard to get people outside of the region to wrap their head around what is going on there because it’s so complicated and the bar of entry for understanding is quite high,” he adds. “With this documentary, we tried to switch our approach where instead of trying to explain or go into the hard details of Myanmar’s history and culture, what we did was focus on the universal, human themes like sovereignty, freedom and missing home.”
	

	This also spoke to our current political moment, where younger generations are taking central roles in political movements across the world. “White Tiger Column” opens IDFA mere weeks after Brazil re-elected Lula following historic demonstrations kickstarted by students from the Fluminense Federal University, and Serbia’s long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić was overthrown by a student-led protest movement in the country’s snap parliamentary elections. Young people were also decisive in the recent midterm elections in the U.S., with the second-highest youth turnout in a midterm election in 30 years.

	“Revolution is on the lips of a lot of people,” says Dickie, with Jantzi adding: “We just hope this can be a portrait of what revolution could look like around the world. If democracy were to fall, would we have the courage and the power to fight? Over the years, there’s been this conversation about Gen Z and Gen Alpha not having what older generations had, but I think this picture of these kids leaving it all behind—video games, comfort—to fight for the future of their country is so beautiful.”

	Dickie intervenes to say that “the Spring Revolution in Myanmar is a very pure grassroots revolution and quite anarchic,” but it is also a “bit of a Catch-22.” “Although it is a beautiful revolution, at the end of the day, it is a revolution. I talk to these guys weekly; they are still in the jungle fighting. People are still dying in the mud. They are still being bombed from the sky. When talking about revolution, you can get caught up in the theory of it and the flowery language, but at the end of the day, this is war.”

	“White Tiger Column” is produced by Tom Edgerton for Lightwood Green in co-production with Nocte Films and Rugio!

title: Oscar Predictions: ‘Cliff Booth’ Readies First Academy Screening, ‘The Odyssey’ Sets Sail and Governors Weekend Gathers Contenders
description: Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predi
body:
Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					Los Angeles, California — NOVEMBER 10: A view of the theater is seen during a special screening of “The Odyssey” making-of documentary and Q&A presented by Universal Pictures at The Steven Spielberg Theater on the Universal Lot 
									2026 Universal Pictures
	




	2027 Academy Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Nov. 12, 2026): A big weekend is ahead, headlined by the 17th Governors Awards on Sunday.

	The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will present honorary Oscars to eight-time nominee Glenn Close, legendary director Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman, Disney’s first Black animator. At the same time, Killer Films producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, longtime champions of independent film, will receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. The ceremony will take place at the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood.

	As always, the Governors Awards double as one of the season’s most important campaign stops. Contenders spend the night working a room filled with the Academy’s governors, three from each of its 19 branches, representing everyone from actors and directors to artisans and executives.

	There’s more going on during the weekend, with many of the year’s mysteries being revealed. 

	On Thursday, Walt Disney Studios’ 65th animated feature “Hexed” will hold its world premiere in Los Angeles, which hopes to shake up a very competitive Oscar category that includes Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” Laika’s “Wildwood” and more. The day before the Governors Awards, Netflix will host the official Academy screening for members for David Fincher’s highly anticipated “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” written by Quentin Tarantino, in which Brad Pitt reprises his Oscar-winning role from “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood” (2019). The film opens in Imax on Nov. 25 ahead of its Dec. 23 streaming debut. This week, Focus Features held its first screenings of Robert Eggers’ medieval gothic horror film “Werwulf” with Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Lily Rose-Depp, with reactions under embargo. 

	All of these events could move the needle for several contenders. But Variety’s predictions track only what’s happened over the past week. So what’s happened?

	Amazon MGM Studios’ “I Play Rocky” has sparked multiple conversations among the studio, the Writers Guild of America, the Academy and the film’s creative team over whether Peter Gamble’s script will compete as an original or adapted screenplay. No determination has been made. Will it matter for its Oscar prospects?

	Kate Berlant and John Early were announced as co-hosts for the 42nd Film Independent Spirit Awards, the annual celebration of the best in independent film and television, which will be held on Saturday, March 6, 2027, at the Hollywood Palladium, which is before the Oscars ceremony and after voting closes.

	Universal officially kicked off the Oscar campaign for Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” this week with “Behind the Scenes of ‘The Odyssey,’” a 75-minute documentary chronicling the making of the $1.8 billion blockbuster. Afterward, star Matt Damon, who plays Odysseus, moderated an hourlong conversation with 12 department heads: producer Emma Thomas, production designer Ruth De Jong, editor Jennifer Lame, composer and songwriter Ludwig Göransson, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, special effects supervisor Scott Fisher, costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, casting director John Papsidera, supervising sound editor Craig Henighan, production sound mixer Willie Burton, head of makeup Luisa Abel and head of hair Gloria Casny.

	This week’s digital column looks at something few people have noticed yet: The Oscars could be barreling toward a repeat of some not-so-great history with another round of #OscarsSoWhite.

	This week’s updates are below.

	The 17th Governors Awards, honoring Close, Scott, Norman, Vachon and Koffler, take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscar shortlists in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlists announced Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, nomination voting runs Jan. 11-15, 2027. The Academy will announce the official Oscar nominations Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars take place Sunday, March 14, 2027, with Conan O’Brien hosting for the third consecutive year. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.

	Projected nomination leaders (films): “The Odyssey” (15); “Dune: Part Three” (12); “La Bola Negra” (11); “Project Hail Mary” (8); “Wild Horse Nine” (7); “The Debut” and “The Invite” (5); “Elsinore” (4); “Werwulf” and “You Can See Everything” (3); “Behemoth!,” “Rose,” “Tender Loving Care” and “Toy Story 5” (2)

	Projected nomination leaders (studios): Universal Pictures (16); A24 (14); Netflix and Warner Bros. (13); Focus Features and Searchlight Pictures (9); Amazon MGM Studios (8); Neon (6); Bleecker Street, Mubi and Sony Pictures Classics (3); Laika and Pixar (2)

            There's apparently no amount of CPR that can save LaTeasha Lunceford's marriage … because she's filed for divorce from Dr. Gregory Lunceford ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, the "Married to Medicine" alum filed divorce papers Tuesday, citing that their marriage is "irretrievably broken with no hope of reconciliation."
      
    
            LaTeasha and Dr. Gregory had been married for more than 3 years, but she says they've been separated since before the filing. She didn’t specify when exactly they split.
      
    
            She's asking for spousal support, saying she "lacks sufficient income and resources to maintain the standard of living established during the marriage" ... noting that her estranged husband makes enough money to be able to pay.
      
    
            In addition to spousal support, LaTeasha is requesting they equitably divide their marital assets, and each keep the cars in their possession.
      
    
            She says if Dr. Gregory pushes back on what she's asking for, he should have to cover her legal fees and court costs.

title: Ken Paxton Trades Campaign Trail for Vaca After Senate Loss
description:
Ken Paxton
                          Goodbye Lone Star State ... Hello Paradise!!!
body:
Ken Paxton
                          Goodbye Lone Star State ... Hello Paradise!!!
                          Jets Off After Bruising Senate Loss
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 12, 2026
                            1:00 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Ken Paxton isn't wasting time sulking over his brutal midterm defeat ... the outgoing Texas Attorney General was spotted ditching the Lone Star State for a getaway with his girlfriend, Tracy Duhon!
      
    
            Pictures and videos obtained by TMZ show Paxton and Duhon strolling through the terminal at San Francisco International Airport Wednesday night. One witness claims the duo was overheard being worried about their bags making it to Fiji.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The escape comes right on the heels of his historic U.S. Senate loss to Democrat James Talarico -- a defeat that handed Democrats their first statewide victory in Texas in over three decades.
      

            It’s also not the first time the pair have turned heads at an airport. Back in July, Paxton and Duhon were caught on camera heading off on an international vacation to Iceland ... sparking major backlash from critics on both sides of the aisle during the height of his campaign.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Looks like the embattled politician decided the best cure for an election night hangover is a tropical beach, a fruity drink, and a whole ocean separating him from Texas politics.
      
    
            Bon voyage, Ken!

title: Ole Miss Monkey Noise Scandal: Alaina Kunes' Father Receives Voicemail Death Threat, Listen
description:
Ole Miss Student Alaina Kunes
                          Read and Hear The Threats She's Receiving
body:
Ole Miss Student Alaina Kunes
                          Read and Hear The Threats She's Receiving
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 12, 2026
                            9:45 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 12, 2026
                                10:21 AM PST
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Alaina Kunes and her family have received numerous alleged threats ... including a shocking voicemail from a person claiming to be an Ole Miss student, promising to hang her if she sees her on campus again.
      
    
            Listen to the voicemail ... which begins with a woman telling Scott Kunes -- Alaina's father -- that she's going to hang his daughter.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            She claims to live in Mississippi and attend the university ... so she promises if she sees Alaina on Monday -- presumably meaning the Monday earlier this week -- then she'd take action into her own hands.
      

            The woman says she plans to "take one for the team" ... presumably meaning she's willing to take the consequences if it means taking out Alaina.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Numerous other people have allegedly sent threats in text and email form as well ... saying they are going to hunt the family down and making sexually charged remarks denigrating Alaina.
      
    
            A spokesperson for Alaina tells TMZ ... “Throughout this week, Alaina and her family have faced intense harassment and threats of violence. At the same time, they are deeply troubled by fake fundraising campaigns circulating online about this incident, as well as the vitriol directed at Jakiyra, Victoria and Kaiyden. Alaina hopes that the hate and hostility will cease and that the Ole Miss community can begin to heal and move forward in unity and peace." 
      
    
            Sources also tell us this voicemail and these messages are just the tip of the iceberg ... claiming there are hundreds more just like these.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we've reported ... Alaina apologized for making monkey noises and gestures in the controversial video caught on an Ole Miss doorbell camera. She insists she did not know who lived there when she made the noises, and the ladies in the clip previously stated were making animal noises at multiple other abodes that night.
      
    
            Due to the constant harassment, Alaina decided to withdraw from school. The other student involved in the video -- Lauren Mayfield -- has not yet apologized ... which may end up earning her a whole bunch of cash.
